Robot Doctor Mechanisms

Arm or slide shakes, overshoots, or runs away

Bounces around the target, overshoots, or slams to full speed. Below are the 5 most common causes on FTC robots, ordered from most to least likely, with how to check and fix each one.

Skip the guesswork — run the interactive diagnosisAbout 6 quick questions narrow this list down to your robot's actual problem.

Quick checks first

  • Does it slam to full speed and blow past the target? It does not slow down near the target. It just keeps going.
  • Does it shake back and forth around the target? Command a position and watch what happens right at the end.
  • If you turn the shaft by hand, does the encoder number in telemetry change smoothly? Print motor.getCurrentPosition() and turn the motor or mechanism by hand.
  • Moving it the "positive" direction by hand, does the count go up? Decide which way is positive (up, out, forward), then move it that way.
  • Does your control code add a gravity term (kG / feedforward)? A constant added to the output for slides, or kCos × cos(angle) for arms.
  • If you draw a marker line across the hub and shaft, does it split after running? Draw one straight line over the hub (or collar) and the shaft, run it a few times, and look again.

Common causes and how to fix them

1 Position control gains are off

Too much P makes it oscillate, too little leaves it short. D is what damps overshoot.

How to fix it 30 min

  1. GM0's tuning order: set I and D to 0, raise P until it oscillates around the target, then add D until the overshoot is gone.
  2. Oscillating around the target means not enough D. Reaching it very slowly means not enough P (or too much D).
  3. Leave I at 0 unless friction stops it short. If you use I, cap it so it cannot wind up.
  4. Use the RoboCodex PID tuner to get a feel for each gain before touching the real robot.

Sources: GM0 · Control loops

2 Encoder counts the wrong way

If the encoder counts down while the motor drives up, the controller pushes harder the wrong way and runs away at full speed.

How to fix it 5 min

  1. Print the encoder in telemetry and move the mechanism by hand in the positive direction. The count should go up.
  2. If it goes down, reverse the motor (setDirection reverses the encoder too), or flip the sign in your code for external encoders.
  3. GM0: a motor that goes full speed regardless of the target is almost always a reversed motor or a bad encoder cable.

Sources: GM0 · Control loops · GM0 · Encoders

3 Encoder cable unplugged, wrong port, or wrong pinout

Encoders only work in the encoder port next to the matching motor port, with a good cable.

How to fix it 10 min

  1. Plug the encoder into the encoder port right next to its motor's power port (same number).
  2. Turn the shaft by hand with telemetry running. If the count never changes, it is hardware.
  3. If the count flickers between 0 and 1, the cable is bad or half seated.
  4. Old NeveRest motors use a different encoder pin order. Use the correct adapter cable.
  5. 5 V Modern Robotics-style encoders need a REV Logic Level Converter on REV hubs.

Sources: GM0 · Encoders · GM0 · Control loops · FTC Docs · Troubleshooting common issues

4 No gravity feedforward

Gravity is a constant load. Without a feedforward term, PID has to fall below the target before it pushes back, so the mechanism sags.

How to fix it 20 min

  1. Vertical slides: add a constant kG to the output. Raise it until the slide just holds still at mid-height.
  2. Arms: gravity changes with angle, so scale the term by cos(angle), with 0° pointing horizontally.
  3. Then tune PID on top for the remaining error.
Feedforward + PID
// vertical slide
double power = pid.calculate(target, slidePos) + kG;

// arm (angle in degrees, 0 = horizontal)
double power = pid.calculate(target, armAngle) + kCos * Math.cos(Math.toRadians(armAngle));

Sources: GM0 · Control loops

5 Hub or collar slipping on the shaft

Set screws work loose and chew the shaft, so the gear or sprocket spins while the shaft does not (or the reverse).

How to fix it 15 min

  1. Mark the shaft and hub with a marker line. If the lines separate after a run, it is slipping.
  2. Switch to clamping hubs and collars, or hex / D-shaft hubs, wherever possible.
  3. If you must use set screws, file a flat on round shafts and use blue threadlocker on metal (never on plastic).
  4. Use nylon locknuts everywhere. Plain nuts vibrate loose.

Sources: GM0 · Building tips · GM0 · Shaft retention
